document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 19-year-old woman has been diagnosed with MELAS syndrome caused by a pathogenic variant in mitochondrial DNA. Her mother has migraines and sensorineural hearing loss and carries the same variant; her father is unaffected. She asks whether her own future children would be at risk, and whether the children of her affected brother would also be at risk. Which pattern of inheritance best explains this disorder?

options.text: Maternal inheritance, with transmission by affected females to all of their offspring

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that disorders caused by pathogenic variants in mitochondrial DNA are maternally inherited by all offspring, because all mitochondria and their associated mitochondrial DNA in the embryo come from the maternal ovum with no paternal contribution. MELAS is given as the example of such a disorder, so she would transmit the variant to all her children while her brother would not transmit it to any of his.

optionExplanations.b: Autosomal dominant inheritance involves a gene on chromosomes 1-22 and would permit transmission by an affected father, which does not occur for mitochondrial DNA variants.
optionExplanations.c: Autosomal recessive inheritance requires pathogenic variants in both copies of an autosomal gene; mitochondrial disorders follow this pattern only when the causative gene is nuclear, such as POLG in Alpers syndrome.
optionExplanations.d: X-linked inheritance involves genes on the X chromosome and typically produces disease that is more common or more severe in males.
optionExplanations.e: Imprinting disorders such as Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes arise from parent-of-origin gene expression on nuclear chromosomes, not from mitochondrial DNA.

questions.question: A 15-year-old girl is referred for primary amenorrhoea and absent breast development. She is 142 cm tall, well below the 3rd percentile, with a short webbed neck, low posterior hairline, broad chest with widely spaced nipples, and an increased carrying angle at the elbows. Her blood pressure is elevated and a systolic murmur suggests a bicuspid aortic valve. Her school performance and intelligence are normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes Turner syndrome (45,X in about half of cases) as presenting with short stature, short webbed neck, low posterior hairline, wide carrying angle, broad chest with widely spaced nipples, coarctation of the aorta or bicuspid aortic valve, increased risk of hypertension, and streak ovaries causing primary amenorrhoea and impaired development of secondary sexual characteristics, with typically normal intelligence. Diagnosis is made by karyotype.

optionExplanations.b: Noonan syndrome also causes short stature and a webbed neck, but is autosomal dominant, affects both sexes, features right-sided congenital heart disease with pulmonary stenosis, and is associated with moderate intellectual disability and delayed puberty rather than streak ovaries.
optionExplanations.c: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) occurs in males and produces a tall, slim build with gynecomastia and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.
optionExplanations.d: Fragile X syndrome causes overgrowth with macrocephaly, prominent jaw, and large ears, and females with a full mutation show intellectual impairment rather than this physical phenotype.
optionExplanations.e: Down syndrome presents with hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, a flat nasal bridge, low IQ, and atrioventricular septal defect.

source.reference: MG6 — Table 3. Common Genetic Disorders Involving the Sex Chromosomes

questions.question: An 18-month-old boy is referred to genetics for global developmental delay. He also has a ventricular septal defect and a cleft palate. Physical examination does not suggest a recognisable aneuploidy syndrome, and there is no family history of a known chromosomal rearrangement such as a translocation. TORCH screening and brain imaging have been arranged. Which is the most appropriate initial genetic investigation?

options.text: Sanger sequencing of a single candidate gene

questions.explanation: In the genetic assessment of a child with physical differences, Toronto Notes directs that chromosomal microarray analysis (SNP array) be performed if there is developmental delay or autism, or two or more congenital anomalies. This boy has developmental delay plus two major anomalies, and microarray can identify small deletions or duplications anywhere in the genome.

optionExplanations.b: Karyotype is advised when a known aneuploidy syndrome is recognised or when there is a family history of a chromosomal rearrangement such as a translocation, neither of which applies here.
optionExplanations.c: FISH is used when a specific aneuploidy syndrome such as trisomy 13, 18, or 21 is suspected, and no such syndrome is suspected on examination.
optionExplanations.d: Sanger sequencing is the gold standard for identifying single nucleotide variants in a gene known to cause a suspected syndrome, which requires a specific clinical hypothesis.
optionExplanations.e: Repeat-primed PCR determines trinucleotide repeat number and is used in diagnostic or predictive testing for repeat expansion disorders.

source.reference: MG5 — Approach to the Patient with Physical Differences: Investigations

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy is referred for delayed motor milestones. He has proximal muscle weakness, a waddling gait, and toe walking, and he uses his hands to climb up his legs when rising from the floor. His calves appear enlarged and firm while his thigh muscles look wasted, and his deep tendon reflexes are diminished. Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated. Which is the most appropriate first-line diagnostic investigation?

options.text: Molecular genetic testing of the dystrophin (DMD) gene

questions.explanation: Proximal weakness by age 3, a positive Gowers' sign, waddling gait, toe walking, calf pseudohypertrophy with thigh wasting, diminished reflexes, and creatine kinase elevated 50-100 times normal describe Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Toronto Notes lists molecular genetic studies of the dystrophin gene (DMD) as the first-line diagnostic test, and notes that genotype-phenotype correlations distinguish Duchenne from the milder Becker muscular dystrophy.

optionExplanations.b: Muscle biopsy is listed among the diagnostic investigations but is not the first-line test now that molecular testing is available.
optionExplanations.c: Electromyography is likewise a supporting investigation rather than the first-line diagnostic test.
optionExplanations.d: Karyotype detects large changes in chromosome number or structure and would not identify a pathogenic variant within the dystrophin gene.
optionExplanations.e: Chromosomal microarray is indicated for developmental delay, autism, or two or more congenital anomalies, and his presentation is a specific X-linked muscular dystrophy phenotype.

questions.question: A 7-day-old breastfed infant is admitted with jaundice, vomiting, poor feeding, and hepatomegaly. Bilateral cataracts are seen on eye examination, liver enzymes are elevated, and blood cultures grow Escherichia coli. The parents are healthy and unrelated, and the newborn screening result has not yet been reported. Which is the most likely underlying metabolic disorder?

options.text: Glycogen storage disease type 1 (von Gierke disease)

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes galactosemia as an autosomal recessive disease, most commonly due to deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase, leading to an inability to process lactose/galactose, with signs of liver and renal failure, jaundice, failure to thrive, and cataracts with ingestion of lactose/galactose, plus an increased risk of sepsis, especially E. coli. Although galactosemia is screened for in many newborn screening programs, affected infants generally present with liver failure and E. coli sepsis before the screening result is reported. Management is elimination of galactose from the diet, including dairy and breast milk, with most infants fed a soy-based diet.

optionExplanations.a: Phenylketonuria produces a baby who is normal at birth and then develops a musty odour, eczema, hypertonia, tremors, intellectual disability, and hypopigmentation from low tyrosine levels, not cataracts with liver failure and E. coli sepsis.
optionExplanations.c: Maple syrup urine disease causes feeding intolerance, failure to thrive, vomiting, lethargy, and a maple syrup odour in the urine and cerumen, without cataracts or a characteristic association with E. coli sepsis.
optionExplanations.d: Glycogen storage disease type 1 typically presents between 3-6 mo of age with hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, poor fasting tolerance, growth failure, and doll-like facies rather than neonatal jaundice with cataracts.
optionExplanations.e: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency is an X-linked urea cycle condition in which infants appear well at birth and then develop reduced oral intake, lethargy, tachypnea, and severe encephalopathy with hyperammonemia and high urinary orotic acid.

source.reference: MG10 — Table 9. Presentation and Management of Select Metabolic Disorders

questions.question: A 41-year-old woman is referred to a hereditary cancer clinic after a diagnosis of breast cancer. At age 30 she had a thyroidectomy for thyroid carcinoma, and her mother was treated for endometrial carcinoma in her forties. No relative has had colorectal cancer, ovarian cancer, sarcoma, or adrenocortical carcinoma, and no polyposis has been documented. Which familial cancer syndrome best accounts for this pattern?

options.text: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists Cowden syndrome, caused by pathogenic variants in PTEN, as the familial cancer syndrome whose associated cancers are breast, thyroid, and endometrial, which is exactly the combination in this family. Recommended screening includes annual thyroid ultrasound at diagnosis, annual comprehensive physical examination from age 18, and colonoscopy every 5 yr from age 30-35, with annual mammography in women from age 30 and consideration of random annual endometrial biopsy and/or ultrasound.

optionExplanations.a: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome, due to BRCA1 or BRCA2 variants, is associated with breast, ovarian, and pancreatic cancer in women and prostate, breast, and pancreatic cancer in men; thyroid carcinoma is not part of this spectrum.
optionExplanations.b: Lynch syndrome, due to MSH2, MLH1, MSH6, PMS2, or EPCAM variants, includes endometrial and breast cancer but is dominated by colorectal cancer and also includes ovarian, renal, pancreatic, hepatobiliary, gastric, and brain tumours, none of which are present here.
optionExplanations.d: Li-Fraumeni syndrome, due to TP53 variants, is associated with breast cancer together with osteosarcoma, leukemia, soft tissue sarcoma, brain tumours, and adrenocortical carcinoma, which this family does not show.
optionExplanations.e: Familial adenomatous polyposis, due to APC variants, causes colorectal and small intestine or stomach tumours and prompts sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy from age 10 once polyps develop.

source.reference: MG7 — Table 5. Examples of Familial Cancer Syndromes
